definition: The transfer of thermal energy through a material by collisions between neighbouring particles (and, in metals, free electrons), from particles with more average kinetic energy to those with less, with no bulk movement of the material.

The property $k$ of a material, in $\text{W m}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$, that sets how fast it conducts thermal energy for a given area and temperature gradient, as in $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = -kA\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$; metals have high values and insulators low ones.
The transfer of thermal energy by the bulk movement of a liquid or gas: warmer fluid usually expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it.
Energy transferred as electromagnetic waves, mostly infrared at everyday temperatures, which every object above absolute zero emits; it needs no medium, so it can cross a vacuum.
